title: 'H-1B Is a Business Model': Trump Official Defends Green-Card Suspensions
excerpt: Labor Department inspector general Anthony D'Esposito says tech companies use H-1B visas to replace American workers, defending the PERM freeze on Microsoft, Adobe and six IT firms.
body:
• Labor Department inspector general Anthony D'Esposito defended the Trump administration's suspension of Microsoft, Adobe and six IT services firms from the PERM green-card process, accusing employers of using H-1B visas "as a business model."
  • The administration's case rests on Microsoft's numbers: about 6,000 workers laid off last year alongside 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.
  • Microsoft disputes the charge, saying 80% of its roughly 6,000 H-1B filings last year were extensions for existing employees, not new hires from abroad.
  • What this means for you: the freeze pauses new and pending PERM filings for the eight named employers (initial pause of up to 180 days while investigations run). Workers keep working on their current H-1B status, and anyone with an approved I-140 is generally less exposed — but check with an immigration attorney before switching employers while your PERM is on hold.

US Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito on Friday publicly defended the Trump administration's suspension of eight major employers from the employment-based green-card pipeline, saying technology companies have converted the H-1B program into a labor-supply strategy at the expense of American workers. Speaking in a video shared on X, D'Esposito said employers should hire foreign workers only as a stopgap while searching for qualified American candidates, and that skilled US graduates were available to fill the roles.

"They are using the H-1B as a business model, and that's wrong. They're taking American jobs away from American workers," D'Esposito said, according to the Hindustan Times, which first detailed his remarks. The intervention makes the department's top watchdog the public face of a crackdown that has escalated over the past three months.

Context & Background

The suspensions target the Permanent Labor Certification program, known as PERM — the mandatory first step for an employer sponsoring an H-1B worker for a green card. Under PERM, a company must demonstrate it could not find a qualified American worker for the role. Eight employers have been frozen out: Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.

https://x.com/EricLDaugh/status/2109051748237054331

The move grew out of "Project Firewall," a Labor Department enforcement initiative launched in September 2025 that has since opened roughly 200 cases and levied millions of dollars in penalties against companies accused of gaming the system. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling has backed the suspensions with longer-run figures: since 2009, Microsoft and Adobe together have received about 230,000 H-1B approvals and 100,000 permanent labor certifications. The White House has also imposed a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions, and nine elite universities — including Harvard, Yale, Stanford and MIT — face investigations over alleged exchange-visitor visa misuse.

Impact & Analysis

The sharpest rhetoric has come from Vice President JD Vance, whose antifraud task force announced the suspensions on October 8. At a White House press conference, Vance said "there has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft," pointing to the layoff and visa arithmetic. He added that for every worker Microsoft laid off, "they replaced that worker with one-and-a-half foreign indentured servants." The administration argues that companies post deliberately weak job advertisements, then use the resulting silence to justify hiring lower-paid foreign workers through a PERM process it describes as a rubber stamp.

Microsoft has pushed back hard. A spokeswoman said most of the company's US employees are American citizens and that of roughly 6,000 H-1B applications filed last fiscal year, 80% covered existing employees seeking extensions or status changes. "We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work," spokeswoman Kate Frischmann said, adding that the company's wages rank among the highest in H-1B filings. Adobe did not immediately respond to press queries.

Diaspora Angle

Indian professionals are the most exposed group in this fight. Indians account for roughly 71% of H-1B beneficiaries — China is a distant second at about 12% — and the suspended firms include the five largest Indian IT services exporters, whose business models depend on moving engineers between countries. TCS, Infosys and Cognizant have each told markets the suspension will not materially disrupt their workforce strategies, but tens of thousands of Indian workers now face frozen green-card timelines.

What's Next / Looking Ahead

Vance has given no end date for the suspensions. "As long as it needs to," he said when asked how long the bans would last. Under federal rules, the department can pause an employer's PERM cases for up to 180 days while investigating, with longer holds possible during a probe — and criminal charges have not been ruled out. Immigration attorneys expect the suspensions to be challenged in court, potentially within days, arguing the administration exceeded its authority. The $100,000 H-1B fee was extended in September 2026 to run through September 21, 2027.
